at gemme sig.explanation: "At gemme sig" means "to hide (oneself)". The small word "sig" must go with it and changes to "mig" for "I": "Jeg gemmer mig bag døren" (I hide behind the door). To save a file, use "at gemme" without "sig": "Jeg gemmer filen" (I save the file).

at genbruge.explanation: "At genbruge" means "to recycle / reuse". The part "gen-" means "again", so it is "at bruge" (to use) again.

at generalisere.explanation: "At generalisere" means "to generalize". To tell someone they are claiming something about everyone after seeing only a few cases, say: "Du generaliserer for meget" (You are generalizing too much).

at genere.explanation: "At genere" means "to bother". To check that you are not in someone's way, ask: "Generer jeg dig?" (Am I bothering you?)

at gengive.explanation: "At gengive" means "to reproduce / render". It is built from "gen-" (again) and "at give" (to give). To say a picture shows a scene, use it for pictures too: "Maleriet gengiver en storm" (The painting shows a storm).

at genkende.explanation: "At genkende" means "to recognize". It is built from "gen-" (again) and "at kende" (to know), so you know someone again. To say you do not know who a person is, say: "Jeg genkender ham ikke" (I do not recognize him).

at gennemføre.explanation: "At gennemføre" means "to carry out". It is built from "gennem" (through) and "at føre" (to lead), so you lead something through to the end. To say someone finished a course of study, say: "Hun har gennemført uddannelsen" (She has completed the degree program).

at gennemgå.explanation: "At gennemgå" means "to go through / review". To say you look at a text point by point, say: "Vi gennemgår kontrakten" (We go through the contract). To say someone lived through something hard, use it for that too: "Hun har gennemgået en stor operation" (She has been through a major operation).

at gennemskue.explanation: "At gennemskue" means "to see through", as in understanding a trick, not looking through glass. To say you understood a lie, say: "Jeg gennemskuede hans løgn" (I saw through his lie).

at genopbygge.explanation: "At genopbygge" means "to rebuild". The part "gen-" means "again", as in "at genstarte" (to restart). To say a city was built up again after a war, say: "Byen blev genopbygget efter krigen" (The city was rebuilt after the war).

at genoplive.explanation: "At genoplive" means "to revive". The part "gen-" means "again", as in "at genskabe" (to recreate). To say you bring an old custom back into use, say: "Vi vil genoplive den gamle tradition" (We want to revive the old tradition).

at genoprette.explanation: "At genoprette" means "to restore". To say a lost connection is working again, say: "Vi har genoprettet forbindelsen" (We have restored the connection). For an old building or painting, use "at restaurere" (to restore): "De restaurerer maleriet" (They are restoring the painting).

at genoptage.explanation: "At genoptage" means "to resume". It is built from "gen-" (again) and "at optage" (to take up). To say someone started work again, say: "Hun har genoptaget sit arbejde" (She has resumed her work).

at genoverveje.explanation: "At genoverveje" means "to reconsider". It is built from "gen-" (again) and "at overveje" (to consider). To ask someone to think again about a choice, say: "Vil du ikke genoverveje det?" (Won't you reconsider?)

at genskabe.explanation: "At genskabe" means "to recreate / restore". It is built from "gen-" (again) and "at skabe" (to create). To say you cannot make an error happen again, say: "Vi kan ikke genskabe fejlen" (We cannot reproduce the error).

at genstarte.explanation: "At genstarte" means "to restart". To give advice about a router, say: "Prøv at genstarte routeren" (Try restarting the router). To say a company starts a business activity again, say: "Firmaet genstarter produktionen" (The company restarts production).

at gentage.explanation: "At gentage" means "to repeat". It is built from "gen-" (again) and "at tage" (to take). To say that something happens again, add "sig" (itself): "Historien gentager sig" (History repeats itself).

at gide.explanation: "At gide" means "to bother / can be bothered". To say you have no energy or wish to do something, say: "Jeg gider ikke" (I can't be bothered). To ask whether someone feels like joining, ask: "Gider du komme med?" (Do you feel like coming along?)

at gifte sig.explanation: "At gifte sig" means "to get married". The small word "sig" must go with it and changes to match who marries: "du gifter dig" (you get married) and "han gifter sig" (he gets married). To say what state you are in, use "gift" (married): "Jeg er gift" (I am married).

at give.explanation: "At give" means "to give". To ask someone to pass you something at the table, say: "Giv mig saltet, tak" (Pass me the salt, please). To say you do not stop trying, use "at give op" (to give up): "Jeg giver ikke op" (I am not giving up).

at give afkald på.explanation: "At give afkald på" means "to give up / renounce". The small word "på" (on) must come right before the thing you give up: "Hun gav afkald på sin løn" (She gave up her pay).

at give efter.explanation: "At give efter" means "to give in". To say that a thing broke under weight, use it for things too: "Isen gav efter" (The ice gave way).

at give en hånd med.explanation: "At give en hånd med" means "to give a hand". To ask for help with a job, say: "Kan du give en hånd med?" (Can you lend a hand?) The word "med" (along) shows that you join in on a job someone is already doing.

at give lov.explanation: "At give lov" means "to give permission". To say a parent allowed something, say: "Min mor gav lov" (My mother gave permission). The word "lov" also means "law", as in "en ny lov" (a new law).

at give op.explanation: "At give op" means "to give up". To tell someone not to quit, say: "Giv ikke op!" (Do not give up!) The small word "op" (up) is in many phrases, such as "at skrive op" (to write down) and "at ringe op" (to call up).

at give sig.explanation: "At give sig" means "to give in / yield". To say you will not back down, say: "Jeg giver mig ikke" (I will not back down). To say pain eases off, use it for pain too: "Smerterne giver sig" (The pain eases off).

at give tilbage.explanation: "At give tilbage" means "to give back". To ask for your own thing back, say: "Giv mig bogen tilbage" (Give me the book back). To bring something back to a shop or library, use "at returnere" (to return): "Jeg returnerer bogen" (I am returning the book).

at glemme.explanation: "At glemme" means "to forget". To say you forgot to bring something, say: "Jeg glemte mine nøgler" (I forgot my keys). To say you forgot to do something, add "at" (to) and a verb: "Jeg glemte at ringe" (I forgot to call).

at glide.explanation: "At glide" means "to slide / slip". To say something slipped by accident, say: "Kniven gled" (The knife slipped).

at glo.explanation: "At glo" means "to stare". It is a blunt word, not a polite one. To challenge someone who is staring at you, say: "Hvad glor du på?" (What are you staring at?)

at glæde.explanation: "At glæde" means "to please / delight". To say news makes you happy, say: "Det glæder mig at høre det" (I am pleased to hear that). Do not mix it up with "at glæde sig til" (to look forward to), where "sig" (oneself) makes you the one who feels it: "Jeg glæder mig til ferien" (I look forward to the vacation).

at glæde sig over.explanation: "At glæde sig over" means "to be happy about". To say you are happy about something that is already here, say: "Han glæder sig over de gode nyheder" (He is happy about the good news). For something in the future, use "at glæde sig til" (to look forward to): "Jeg glæder mig til ferien" (I look forward to the vacation).

at glæde sig til.explanation: "At glæde sig til" means "to look forward to". The small word "sig" changes with the person: "Vi glæder os til festen" (We look forward to the party). For something that is already here, use "at glæde sig over" (to be happy about): "Hun glæder sig over resultatet" (She is happy about the result).

at gløde.explanation: "At gløde" means "to glow". To say a person is full of a strong feeling, use it for people too: "Hun gløder af stolthed" (She glows with pride).

at gnave.explanation: "At gnave" means "to gnaw". To say a worry keeps bothering you, use it for thoughts too: "Tanken gnavede i mig" (The thought gnawed at me).

at gnide.explanation: "At gnide" means "to rub". To say you rub cream into your skin, add "ind" (in): "at gnide creme ind" (to rub in cream).

at godkende.explanation: "At godkende" means "to approve". It is built from "god" (good) and "at kende" (to know). To say a plan has been approved, say: "De har godkendt planen" (They have approved the plan).

at godtage.explanation: "At godtage" means "to accept". It is built from "god" (good) and "at tage" (to take). To say you do not take an excuse as good enough, say: "Skolen godtager ikke den undskyldning" (The school does not accept that excuse).

at google.explanation: "At google" means "to google". To say you will look something up right away, say: "Jeg googler det lige" (I will just google it).

at grave.explanation: "At grave" means "to dig". To say something is dug out of the ground, add "op" (up): "Hunden graver en knogle op" (The dog digs up a bone).

at gribe.explanation: "At gribe" means "to grab / catch". To say someone took hold of something with the hand, say: "Han greb min arm" (He grabbed my arm).

at gribe ind.explanation: "At gribe ind" means "to intervene". It is built from "at gribe" (to grab) and "ind" (in), as if you reach into the situation. To say someone stepped in to stop a problem, say: "Politiet greb ind" (The police stepped in).

at grille.explanation: "At grille" means "to grill". To say you are grilling without naming the food, say: "Vi griller i aften" (We are grilling tonight).

at grine.explanation: "At grine" means "to laugh". To say you laughed, say: "Vi grinede meget" (We laughed a lot). To say who you laugh at, add "af" (at): "Hvorfor griner du af mig?" (Why are you laughing at me?)

at gro.explanation: "At gro" means "to grow", as in plants coming up from the ground. To say plants come up, say: "Græsset gror" (The grass is growing). For a child getting taller or something getting bigger, use "at vokse" (to grow bigger): "Barnet vokser" (The child is growing).

at gruble.explanation: "At gruble" means "to brood / ponder". To say someone sits and thinks for a long time, say: "Han sidder og grubler" (He is sitting there brooding).

at gruppere.explanation: "At gruppere" means "to group". It comes from the noun "en gruppe" (a group). To say you put things into groups, say: "Jeg grupperer billederne i mapper" (I group the pictures into folders).

at græde.explanation: "At græde" means "to cry", as in weeping. To ask someone why they are crying, say: "Hvorfor græder du?" (Why are you crying?) To say what made you cry, add "af" (from): "Jeg græd af glæde" (I cried with joy).

at gynge.explanation: "At gynge" means "to swing". To say a boat moves gently on the water, say: "Båden gynger på bølgerne" (The boat sways on the waves). To swing a club, use "at svinge" (to swing): "Han svinger køllen" (He swings the club).

at gå.explanation: "At gå" means "to go / walk". To say you are leaving, say: "Jeg går nu" (I am leaving now). To say how things are going, say: "Det går godt" (It is going well). To say a bus runs, say: "Bussen går hver time" (The bus runs every hour). To go by car, use "at køre" (to drive): "Vi kører til Aarhus" (We drive to Aarhus).

at gå af.explanation: "At gå af" means "to resign / go off". To say someone gives up a post, say: "Hun går af som formand" (She resigns as chair). To say you leave a bus or train, say: "Jeg går af ved næste stop" (I get off at the next stop). To say an alarm clock rings, say: "Alarmen gik af" (The alarm went off).

at gå agurk.explanation: "At gå agurk" means "to go crazy". Literally, it is "to go cucumber" ("en agurk" is a cucumber). To tell someone they are driving you crazy, say: "Du får mig til at gå agurk!" (You are driving me crazy!)

at gå amok.explanation: "At gå amok" means "to go berserk". To say a person lost control in anger, say: "Han gik amok på kontoret" (He went berserk in the office).

at gå en tur.explanation: "At gå en tur" means "to go for a walk". To say where you walk, add the place after it: "gå en tur i parken" (go for a walk in the park). The words "en tur" also mean "a trip", as in "en tur til Aarhus" (a trip to Aarhus).

at gå forbi.explanation: "At gå forbi" means "to pass by". The small word "forbi" (past) goes with other verbs too: "Bilen kører forbi" (The car drives past).

at gå fra hinanden.explanation: "At gå fra hinanden" means "to break up". Literally, it is "to go from each other", and "hinanden" means "each other". To say a couple separated, say: "Mine forældre gik fra hinanden, da jeg var ti" (My parents split up when I was ten).

at gå galt.explanation: "At gå galt" means "to go wrong". To say a plan failed, say: "Planen gik galt" (The plan went wrong). To say an answer is wrong, use "forkert" (wrong): "Svaret er forkert" (The answer is wrong).

at gå glip af.explanation: "At gå glip af" means "to miss out on". To say you did not get to be part of an event, say: "Hun gik glip af festen" (She missed out on the party). To say you were too late for a bus, use "at misse" (to miss): "Jeg missede bussen" (I missed the bus).

at gå hjem.explanation: "At gå hjem" means "to go home". To go home by car, use "at køre hjem" (to drive home): "Vi kører hjem" (We drive home). To go home by any means, use "at tage hjem" (to head home): "Jeg tager hjem nu" (I am heading home now).

at gå i biografen.explanation: "At gå i biografen" means "to go to the movies". Literally, it is "to go in the movie theater". To suggest it in a shorter way, say: "Skal vi gå i bio?" (Shall we go to the movies?)

at gå i gang med.explanation: "At gå i gang med" means "to get started on". The small word "med" (with) goes before the task you start: "Hun gik i gang med maden" (She got started on the food). When no task follows, leave "med" out: "Vi er gået i gang" (We have started).

at gå i panik.explanation: "At gå i panik" means "to panic". Literally, it is "to go into panic". To tell someone to stay calm, use "at bevare roen" (to stay calm): "Bevar roen!" (Stay calm!)

at gå i seng.explanation: "At gå i seng" means "to go to bed". Falling asleep is different, so use "at falde i søvn" (to fall asleep): "Jeg faldt i søvn i sofaen" (I fell asleep on the sofa).

at gå i stykker.explanation: "At gå i stykker" means "to break". To say your phone stopped working, say: "Min telefon gik i stykker" (My phone broke). To say you broke something yourself, use "at ødelægge" (to ruin): "Jeg ødelagde telefonen" (I ruined the phone).

at gå i stå.explanation: "At gå i stå" means "to come to a standstill". To say a machine stopped working, say: "Maskinen gik i stå" (The machine stopped). To say your mind went blank, say: "Jeg gik helt i stå" (My mind went completely blank).

at gå igennem.explanation: "At gå igennem" means "to go through". To say you walk from one side of a place to the other, say: "Vi gik igennem skoven" (We went through the forest). To say you go over something step by step, put the thing before "igennem": "Vi går opgaven igennem" (We go over the task).

at gå ind.explanation: "At gå ind" means "to go in". The small word "ind" (in) is for going in: "Hun går ind i butikken" (She walks into the shop). To say someone is already inside, use "inde" (inside): "Han er inde i huset" (He is inside the house).

at gå ind for.explanation: "At gå ind for" means "to be in favor of". To say you back an idea, say: "De går ind for flere cykelstier" (They are in favor of more bike lanes). To say you are against something, use "at gå imod" (to go against): "Jeg går imod forslaget" (I am against the proposal).

at gå med til.explanation: "At gå med til" means "to agree to". The small word "til" (to) comes before what you agree to: "Jeg går med til forslaget" (I agree to the proposal).

at gå ned.explanation: "At gå ned" means "to go down". To say the sun sets, use it for the sun: "Solen går ned" (The sun sets). To say you go down to a lower floor, say: "Jeg går ned i kælderen" (I go down to the basement).

at gå op.explanation: "At gå op" means "to go up". To say the sun rises, use it for the sun: "Solen går op" (The sun rises). To say a sum comes out right, say: "Regnestykket går op" (The sum adds up).

at gå op for.explanation: "At gå op for" means "to dawn on". To say who realizes something, put that person after "for": "Det gik op for mig, at jeg tog fejl" (It dawned on me that I was wrong).

at gå over åen efter vand.explanation: "At gå over åen efter vand" means "to make things unnecessarily complicated". Literally, it is "to go over the stream for water", as if you cross a stream to fetch water when there is water close by.

related.da: at gøre en myg til en elefant
related.en: to make a mountain out of a molehill

at gå på café.explanation: "At gå på café" means "to go to a café". Danish says "på café" (literally, "on café") with no "en" (a) in front of "café". To suggest it to a friend, say: "Skal vi gå på café?" (Shall we go to a café?)

related.en: to go out on the town

at gå på nerverne.explanation: "At gå på nerverne" means "to get on someone's nerves". Literally, it is "to go on the nerves". To name the person who is annoyed, put that person right after "går" (goes): "Larmen går mig på nerverne" (The noise gets on my nerves).

at gå på pension.explanation: "At gå på pension" means "to retire". The word "pension" also means the money paid to a person who has retired: "Han får pension" (He gets a pension).

at gå rundt.explanation: "At gå rundt" means "to walk around". To say you walk around a place, add "om" (around) before the place: "Vi gik rundt om søen" (We walked around the lake). The small word "rundt" (around) goes with other verbs too: "Børnene løber rundt" (The children run around).

at gå som katten om den varme grød.explanation: "At gå som katten om den varme grød" means "to beat around the bush". Literally, it is "to go like the cat around the hot porridge", a picture of a cat circling food that is too hot to eat.

at gå som smurt.explanation: "At gå som smurt" means "to go smoothly". Literally, it is "to go like greased", and "smurt" comes from "at smøre" (to grease). To say a plan worked without trouble, say: "Alt gik som smurt" (Everything went smoothly).

at gå tabt.explanation: "At gå tabt" means "to be lost". To say a letter disappeared, say: "Brevet gik tabt" (The letter was lost). To say you lost something yourself, use "at miste" (to lose): "Jeg mistede min nøgle" (I lost my key).

at gå til.explanation: "At gå til" means "to go to (regularly)". To say you attend a hobby or class regularly, say: "Jeg går til svømning" (I go to swimming lessons). To ask how something happened, use the question: "Hvordan gik det til?" (How did that happen?)

at gå til eksamen.explanation: "At gå til eksamen" means "to take an exam". To say when you sit it, say: "Hun går til eksamen i morgen" (She takes an exam tomorrow). To say you study for it, use "at læse til eksamen" (to study for an exam): "Jeg læser til eksamen" (I am studying for the exam).

at gå tilbage.explanation: "At gå tilbage" means "to go back". To drive back, use "at køre tilbage" (to drive back): "Vi kører tilbage i morgen" (We drive back tomorrow). To say numbers are falling, use it for that too: "Salget går tilbage" (Sales are going down).

at gå ud.explanation: "At gå ud" means "to go out". To ask someone to go out for the evening, say: "Skal vi gå ud i aften?" (Shall we go out tonight?) To say a light stopped shining, say: "Lyset gik ud" (The light went out).

at gå ud fra.explanation: "At gå ud fra" means "to assume". The words "ud fra" also mean "based on" in other sentences: "Ud fra tallene ser det godt ud" (Based on the numbers, it looks good).

at gå ud med.explanation: "At gå ud med" means "to go out with". To say two people are dating, say: "Hun går ud med Peter" (She is going out with Peter). To say you take a dog for a walk, say: "Jeg går ud med hunden" (I am taking the dog out).

at gå videre.explanation: "At gå videre" means "to move on". To say someone has left a past relationship or event behind, say: "Hun er gået videre" (She has moved on).

at gå væk.explanation: "At gå væk" means "to go away". The command "Gå væk!" (Go away!) is a blunt order. To say someone walked off, say: "Han gik væk uden at sige farvel" (He walked off without saying goodbye).

at gætte.explanation: "At gætte" means "to guess". To name your guess, add "på" (on): "Jeg gætter på Peter" (I am guessing Peter). To start telling someone surprising news, say: "Gæt hvad!" (Guess what!)

at gø.explanation: "At gø" means "to bark". The present form "gør" is spelled exactly like "gør" from "at gøre" (to do). For barking, say: "Hunden gør" (The dog barks). For doing, say: "Jeg gør det" (I do it).

at gøre.explanation: "At gøre" means "to do". To avoid repeating a verb, use it in place of that verb: "Jeg læser, og det gør hun også" (I am reading, and she does too). To say you make something, such as food, use "at lave" (to make): "Jeg laver mad" (I am cooking).

at gøre det forbi.explanation: "At gøre det forbi" means "to end it (a relationship)". To name the person you ended it with, add "med" (with): "Hun gjorde det forbi med ham" (She ended it with him). To say it with another phrase, use "at slå op" (to break up): "Han slog op med hende" (He broke up with her).

at gøre en dyd af nødvendigheden.explanation: "At gøre en dyd af nødvendigheden" means "to make a virtue of necessity". In it, "en dyd" means "a virtue" and "nødvendigheden" means "the necessity".

related.da: at gøre det bedste ud af det
related.en: to make the best of it

related.da: at gøre gode miner til slet spil
related.en: to put on a brave face

related.da: at bide i det sure æble

at gøre færdig.explanation: "At gøre færdig" means "to finish". To say you finish a task, say: "Jeg gør opgaven færdig" (I am finishing the assignment). To say you are done yourself, use "at blive færdig" (to be done): "Jeg bliver færdig klokken fem" (I will be done at five).

at gøre grin med.explanation: "At gøre grin med" means "to make fun of". The small word "med" (with) goes before the person you make fun of: "Hun gør grin med mig" (She makes fun of me).

at gøre indtryk.explanation: "At gøre indtryk" means "to make an impression". To say who was affected, add "på" (on) before that person: "Filmen gjorde stort indtryk på mig" (The film made a big impression on me).

at gøre klar.explanation: "At gøre klar" means "to get ready". To say you prepare something, say: "Jeg gør maden klar" (I am getting the food ready). To say you prepare yourself, add "mig" (myself): "Jeg gør mig klar" (I am getting myself ready).

at gøre noget ved.explanation: "At gøre noget ved" means "to do something about". To tell someone to act, say: "Gør noget!" (Do something!) To say what you act on, put it after "ved": "Jeg vil gøre noget ved støjen" (I want to do something about the noise).
